About: a superconducting sample in a uniform applied field

Source

Concept
A declared Nb-like superconducting sample in a uniform applied field, driven by three sliders: the temperature T, the applied field B, and the Ginzburg–Landau parameter κ = λL/ξ.
Serves
Declared material constants: Tc = 9.25 K, Bc(0) = 200 mT, cross-section A = 1 µm². A is the face perpendicular to B — seen edge-on in this cross-section view, not the drawn rectangle.
Model limits
The phase here is a pure function of the three sliders — no hysteresis, no flux pinning, no history. Real magnets pin flux; this declared model does not. The count n uses the flux of the applied field through A, which is exact only for B ≫ Bc1; and the GL log estimate for Bc1 is not modelled for κ ≤ 1.

Pedagogy principles applied

Target the misconception structurally"Field stays frozen in" is a selectable choice whose rebuttal appears only if chosen — never as standing prose.
Operational numbersB is compared against Bc1 and Bc2 in the same unit (mT), and n is counted on screen as well as read.
Stable frameThe phase-diagram axes are fixed (0–12 K, 0–500 mT) so moving κ visibly moves the curves, never the scale.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The sample, edge-on

Let’s meet the sample. It sits at 12 K in 50 mT, drawn in cross-section. The applied field runs straight down the page — trace one blue line and watch it pass straight through the body. One claim holds this whole sim together: below its boundary curve a superconductor holds the field out, and whatever gets back in is quantised. We’ll test both halves.

2 · Cooling in a field

Right now the lines run straight through the warm sample. Suppose you cool it to 4.2 K at the same 50 mT — what do you think happens to the field inside?

3 · Cool it

Let’s see. Drag T from 12 K down to 4.2 K. Watch the interior, and the thin green skin λ at the surface where B dies away inward. You’ll notice the phase diagram and the boundary readout are now open too. So what did the interior do?

4 · Letting the field back in

Now let’s go the other way. The interior is empty at 120 mT. Suppose you warm the sample slowly at fixed B — how do you think the field gets back inside?

5 · Three witnesses

Time to check. Warm T past 8 K, then cool back to 4.2 K. Keep your eyes on three things: the interior, the dot against the boundary curve, and the gap Δ in the Sample state panel. What did the three of them do?

6 · What gets back in

Now for the second half of the claim. κ = λL/ξ decides the type. Suppose you raise κ to 1.50 (type II), with B lying between Bc1(T) and Bc2(T). What do you think the cross-section would show then?

7 · Count the tubes

Let’s look. Keep T = 4.2 K and B = 50 mT, and drag κ up to 1.50. Two new boundary curves appear — Bc1(T) and Bc2(T) — with the old Bc(T) now dashed between them. Can you count the tubes threading the body? Then read the Flux panel.

8 · Doubling the field

So the sample is in the mixed state at B = 50 mT. Now suppose you double B to 100 mT, still below Bc2. What do you think the vortex count does?

9 · Double it

Let’s put it to the test. Drag B to 100 mT and read the count, then compare it with the 24 you counted at 50 mT — the earlier value is pinned beside it in the Flux panel. What does n read now?

10 · The one thing

Let’s bring it all together. Below its boundary curve a superconductor holds the field out; whatever gets back in is quantised. You never touched T — so why did the count still double? And here’s one to take away: an MRI magnet wound from type-II wire at 3 T — what does its cross-section hold?

The Physics

The superconductor · a complete revision sheet · the field thrown out, the flux in lumps

A superconductor isn't a wire with the last of its resistance taken away. It's a state of matter that throws the magnetic field out of itself — and takes it back only in countable lumps.

01

What can a superconductor do that a perfect conductor cannot?

Both samples cooled from 12 K to 4.2 K in the same 50 mT — same history, opposite interiors. The superconductor drawn is type I (κ = 0.50, as in the guided inquiry); at the sim’s default κ = 1.50, 50 mT is already above Bc1 = 30.35 mT and some flux gets in as tubes — ch 05’s story. The bent lines are computed exactly, not sketched: the surface is itself a field line, so no flux crosses it.
  • A perfect conductor only forbids the field from changing. Zero resistance means no electric field inside, so ∂B/∂t = 0 — whatever was there when the resistance vanished is frozen in forever.
  • A superconductor forbids the field from being there at all: B = 0 inside, reached by expelling flux it was already holding. Cool it in a field and it empties its own interior. That is the Meissner effect, and it is a separate fact from zero resistance.
  • The expulsion is done by a screening current Js circulating in a thin surface skin — out of the page on the left face, into it on the right, the sense that exactly cancels B inside. The Sample state panel names it whenever there is a field to screen.
  • So the state is a phase, not a history. The same (T, B, κ) always gives the same picture, whichever route you took to get there.
The whole distinction in one line: the perfect conductor pins dB/dt, the superconductor pins B.
02

How far into the sample does the field get — and what are λL and ξ?

  • The sim's κ slider is labelled κ = λL/ξ and never says what the two lengths are. λL, the London penetration depth, is the first: the field does not stop dead at the surface but dies away exponentially inward, B(x) = Bsurface·e−x/λL. λL is that decay length — the green skin the sim draws, tens of nanometres in a real metal.
  • ξ, the coherence length, is the second: superconductivity cannot switch on instantly either. The pair wavefunction needs a distance ξ to climb from zero to full strength, which is also the size of the normal core at the centre of a vortex.
  • κ is just their ratio, and it is the only thing that decides the type. In this sim ξ is held fixed and the κ slider stretches λL = κξ — which is why moving κ moves the skin and the boundary curves but never the drawn size of a quantum.
  • A surface between normal and superconducting material costs energy when ξ > λL and pays when λL > ξ. Break-even is exactly κ = 1/√2 = 0.70711: below it the sample keeps flux out whole (type I); above it the sample makes as much surface as it can, and the flux that enters subdivides into vortices (type II).
The London equation and its solution: B falls off over λL, which is what the green skin in the sim is showing.
One ratio, one threshold — the number marked on the sim's κ range.
The two lengths at a normal/superconducting surface, drawn at the sim's two κ settings with ξ held fixed. Below κ = 1/√2 a surface costs energy, so the sample keeps flux out whole; above it a surface pays, so the flux that enters subdivides.
03

Where is the boundary — and which side of it am I on right now?

One parabola cuts the whole (T, B) plane, and it dies exactly at Tc.
In type II the single curve becomes two, both evaluated at Bc(T) — the declared model, quoted at the sim's defaults.
T B κ

These are the sim's real sliders — drag here and the sample, the phase diagram and the readouts all follow.

  • The thermodynamic boundary is a parabola in temperature: 200 mT at absolute zero, 158.77 mT at the 4.2 K default, 50.40 mT at 8 K, and exactly zero at Tc = 9.25 K. Warming at fixed B carries the operating dot to the curve, and the field is in — all at once, not by seeping.
  • In type II that curve splits: Bc1 is where flux starts to get in, Bc2 is where superconductivity finally dies. At κ = 1.50 and 4.2 K they are 30.35 mT and 336.80 mT, with Bc itself sitting between them — which is why the sim draws Bc dashed once there are two real boundaries.
  • Crossing the curve is one event with three witnesses: the interior fills, the dot meets the curve, and Δ drops to zero — all at the same temperature, because they are three readings of a single phase change.
The sim's own diagram, computed on its fixed axes — 0–12 K and 0–500 mT, so only the curves move when κ moves. The ringed dot is the same operating point in both, (4.2 K, 50 mT): vortex state at κ = 1.50, Meissner at κ = 0.50.
The whole phase rule. Type I has one boundary and two states; type II has two boundaries and three.
04

What is the energy gap, and what has it got to do with the field?

Δ(T) computed from the sim's own tanh interpolation, with the 4.2 K default and the 8 K point marked. Flat near T = 0, then off a cliff at Tc — the gap closes at the transition, never before it — and 2Δ(0)/kBTc = 3.528, the weak-coupling BCS value.
  • Electrons bind into pairs, and breaking a pair costs a minimum energy 2Δ. The gap is what protects the paired state from small scatterings. The resistance is exactly zero because all the pairs share one phase-coherent state: a current it carries cannot be slowed one electron at a time.
  • Δ(0) = 1.764 kBTc = 1.406 meV for this Tc = 9.25 K material, and the ratio 2Δ(0)/kBTc = 3.528 is weak-coupling BCS theory’s prediction for every weak-coupling superconductor — a prediction, not a fitted constant. Strong-coupling metals sit higher (real Nb ≈ 3.8, Pb ≈ 4.3); this sim uses the weak-coupling value.
  • Δ is flat near T = 0 and falls off a cliff at Tc: 1.346 meV at 4.2 K is still 95.7% of its zero-temperature value, 0.839 meV at 8 K, and exactly 0 from 9.25 K on. The gap closes at the transition, never before it.
  • One honest caveat the panel carries for you: the curve is the zero-field BCS gap. In the mixed state the readout relabels itself Δ (between cores), because the gap survives only in the material between the tubes; a field-driven normal state has no gap at all.
The gap, its weak-coupling ratio, and the interpolation the sim evaluates at every temperature.
05

Why does what gets back in come in lumps?

The quantum, the count, and the field it takes to add one more tube — the sim's Flux panel in three lines.
  • All the pairs share one wavefunction. Carry it once round a flux tube and the phase has to come back to itself, which quantises the enclosed flux in units of Φ₀ = h/2e = 2.0678 × 10⁻¹⁵ Wb. The 2e is the pair charge — that is why the quantum is this size and not twice it.
  • So the sample cannot hold 24.18 tubes. It holds n = ⌊B·A/Φ₀⌋ = 24. The floor is the physics, not a rounding: 24.18 quanta of applied flux is 24 whole vortices.
  • Every tube is identical and carries exactly one Φ₀; a tube never fattens. Double B to 100 mT and the quotient runs 24.18 → 48.36, so the count runs 24 → 48, exactly in proportion.
  • Between those doublings it is a staircase, not a ramp: one more tube each time B grows by Φ₀/A = 2.0678 mT, and never a fraction of one.
The same rule twice — magnified around the 50 mT default, and over the first 110 mT of the 0–500 mT slider (4.2 K, κ = 1.50). A staircase, not a ramp: one more whole tube every Φ₀/A = 2.0678 mT, never a fraction of one. Below Bc1 the sample is Meissner and holds none; because n counts the applied field's flux through A, the mixed state opens 14 tubes deep at Bc1, and the count climbs to 162 just below Bc2 = 336.80 mT, where the sample goes normal.
06

What is this model not telling you?

  • n counts the applied field's flux through A. That is exact only for B ≫ Bc1. Right where the mixed state opens the formula already gives ⌊Bc1·A/Φ₀⌋ ≈ 14 tubes, not one — a real sample admits its first vortex singly at Bc1, and this model cannot show that.
  • The Bc1 estimate has a hole in it. The logarithmic form Bc·lnκ/(√2κ) is only valid for κ > 1; between 1/√2 and 1 the logarithm degenerates and the estimate goes negative. The sim says so, pins Bc1 = Bc across that window and greys the curve — a gap in the model, not a property of the material.
  • The drawn frame is a side view. The applied field lies in the plane of the page, so the counting face A = 1 µm² is the face perpendicular to B, seen edge-on — not the rectangle you are looking at. Vortices are continuous flux tubes running the whole way through, one quantum each. Drawing them as dots would be the view along B, and one picture cannot be both.
  • No history, anywhere. The phase here is a pure function of (T, B, κ): no hysteresis, no flux pinning. Real type-II magnets pin flux hard — that is exactly what makes them useful — and this declared model does not.
07

The traps they'll set for you

  • "A superconductor is just a perfect conductor, so the field it had stays trapped inside." Perfect conductivity alone would freeze it in. The defining observation is the opposite: cooled in a field, the sample empties itself.
  • "Superconductivity is destroyed as soon as B passes Bc1." Bc1 is only where flux begins to get in. The material between the tubes stays superconducting all the way to Bc2 — 336.80 mT at the defaults, eleven times Bc1.
  • "Double the field and each vortex just carries more flux." The quantum cannot grow: Φ₀ = h/2e is fixed by nature. More flux can only mean more tubes, 24 becoming 48.
  • "n = 24.18, so call it 24." It is not a rounding. ⌊·⌋ is the physics — 24.9 quanta of applied flux is still 24 whole vortices, and the 25th appears only when B reaches the next multiple of 2.0678 mT.
08

Ninety-second self-test

Set B to exactly 0 at 4.2 K. What does the vortex count read, and what is the sample doing?

n = ⌊0·A/Φ₀⌋ = 0, and the Flux panel shows "—" because there is no vortex state to count in. The sample is superconducting with Δ = 1.346 meV and simply nothing to expel — the Meissner state with zero applied field, which is why the panel says so in words rather than drawing an empty interior as an achievement.

Halve the sample's face from 1 µm² to 0.5 µm² at a fixed 50 mT. What happens to n, and to the field needed for one more tube?

n halves: B·A/Φ₀ goes 24.18 → 12.09, so ⌊·⌋ = 12. And Φ₀/A doubles to 4.136 mT, so the staircase becomes twice as coarse — half as many tubes, each needing twice the field increment to add the next. Φ₀ itself does not move; it is h/2e, a constant of nature, not of the sample.

At 4.2 K you set κ = 0.60 and B = 100 mT. Which state, and why is there no vortex answer?

κ = 0.60 is below 1/√2 = 0.70711, so the material is type I: there is one boundary, Bc(4.2) = 158.77 mT, and 100 mT is under it — Meissner. A vortex state needs a normal/superconducting surface that pays for itself, and that only happens above κ = 1/√2. The readout reports Bc1 and Bc2 as absent rather than as zero, because they do not exist here.
